items.meta: Medieval to Augustan British Canon

fields.label: List I (Works)
fields.value:
1. The Canterbury Tales
2. The Faerie Queene
3. Paradise Lost
4. Gulliver's Travels

fields.label: List II (Matched Authors — Answer Key)
fields.value:
1. The Canterbury Tales  →  Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1387)
2. The Faerie Queene  →  Edmund Spenser (1590–96)
3. Paradise Lost  →  John Milton (1667)
4. Gulliver's Travels  →  Jonathan Swift (1726)

fields.label: Board Summary Explanation
fields.value:
• The Canterbury Tales was composed by Geoffrey Chaucer, introducing Middle English estates satire and the heroic couplet.
• The Faerie Queene is an allegorical epic romance by Edmund Spenser composed in nine-line Spenserian stanzas.
• Paradise Lost is a monumental twelve-book Christian epic in unrhymed blank verse by John Milton.
• Gulliver's Travels is a celebrated four-part Menippean prose satire by Anglo-Irish author Jonathan Swift.

• The Duchess of Malfi is Webster's harrowing Jacobean tragedy centered on corruption, incestuous jealousy, and court villainy.

• Horace declared in Ars Poetica that the aim of poets is either to benefit, or to please, or to unite both pleasure and utility.
• Keats defined this supreme poetic virtue as being 'capable of being in uncertainties, mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact and reason'.

fields.label: List II (Matched Definitions — Answer Key)
fields.value:

3. Litotes  →  Deliberate understatement by asserting the negative of its contrary

fields.label: Board Summary Explanation
fields.value:

• An ironic understatement asserting a positive by denying its opposite, e.g. 'no small tempest' or 'he is not ungenerous'.
• A compressed juxtaposition of two starkly conflicting words to generate new meaning, e.g. 'darkness visible' or 'pleasing pain'.

fields.label: List II (Matched Authors — Answer Key)
fields.value:
1. Preface to Lyrical Ballads (1800/1802)  →  William Wordsworth
2. A Defence of Poetry (1821)  →  Percy Bysshe Shelley
3. Tradition and the Individual Talent (1919)  →  T. S. Eliot
4. The Art of Fiction (1884)  →  Henry James

fields.label: Board Summary Explanation
fields.value:
• Wordsworth called for poetry written in 'a selection of language really used by men' and originating from emotion recollected in tranquillity.
• Shelley replied to Thomas Love Peacock's 'Four Ages of Poetry', famously concluding that 'poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world'.
• Eliot argued that poetry is not a turning loose of emotion, but an escape from emotion, expounding his impersonal theory of poetry.
• Henry James responded to Walter Besant, defining the novel as a living personal impression of life free from moralistic straightjackets.

2. Synchronic vs. Diachronic Linguistics  →  Ferdinand de Saussure
3. Communicative Competence  →  Dell Hymes
4. Speech Acts (Locutionary, Illocutionary, Perlocutionary)  →  J. L. Austin

fields.label: Board Summary Explanation
fields.value:
• Chomsky distinguished innate linguistic knowledge of grammar (competence) from actual real-world language production (performance).
• Saussure separated the study of language at a static point in time (synchronic) from its historical evolution across time (diachronic).
• Hymes introduced the ethnography of communication (SPEAKING model) showing that language competence requires knowing when to speak and what to say appropriately.
• Austin established performative language in How to Do Things with Words, distinguishing saying something from the act performed in saying it.

• Genette replaced the vague term 'point of view' with focalization to analyze the perspective through which narrative events are filtered.
• Booth introduced this foundational concept in The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961) for narrators whose norms diverge from the implied author's.
• Bakhtin defined the chronotope as the intrinsic connectedness of spatial and temporal relationships artistically expressed in literature.

• Heidegger investigated fundamental ontology through human existence (Dasein) and the ready-to-hand nature of worldly tools.

• Kuntaka defined vakrokti (deviant, artistic utterance) as the defining soul and indispensable life-breath of poetic language.
• Kshemendra declared that without auchitya (absolute propriety of emotion, ornament, and context), all poetic virtue is ruined.

• Jameson identified pastiche as the imitation of dead styles without satirical purpose, reflecting late capitalism's depthlessness.
• Lyotard argued that modern science and politics legitimized themselves through sweeping metanarratives that postmodernity no longer credits.
• Deleuze and Guattari opposed arboreal hierarchical thought with the non-linear, multi-directional connectivity of the botanical rhizome.

fields.value:

• Ettinger proposed the matrixial gaze as a co-poetic, non-phallic sphere of shared resonance and relational compassion before separation.
• Haraway used the hybrid figure of the cyborg to dismantle essentialist binaries of nature/culture, male/female, and human/machine.
• Crenshaw coined intersectionality in 1989 to demonstrate how race, gender, and class discrimination intersect and compound systemic marginalization.

fields.label: Board Summary Explanation

• Benjamin argued that a translation must not communicate meaning but touch upon the echo of the original to release pure language.
